title: The risks of food colouring, as UP steps up scrutiny
syllabus: GS2 › Issues relating to health; Government policies and interventions · GS3 › Food processing (food safety) · GS4 › Public health versus livelihoods
summary: After industrial dyes were found in chutney, UP's food safety department has banned colours in chutneys and non-food dyes like Rhodamine-B in street food before Diwali.
evolution: Food Safety and Standards Act: penalties for sub-standard, misbranded and unsafe food.
Food Additives Regulations allow only listed colours, by food category and within limits.
UP issues detailed guidelines after non-food industrial dyes are found in chutney.
ideas: Hidden harm in everyday food: industrial dyes like Rhodamine-B, meant for textiles and paper, colour chutneys, cotton candy and kebabs, mostly at roadside stalls in small cities.
Industrial dyes such as Rhodamine-B in street food show that food adulteration is a silent public-health threat.
Slow, unseen damage: long-term intake can cause liver damage or cancer, so vendors and buyers underrate the risk.
Because harm from banned dyes builds slowly, neither vendors nor consumers see the danger.
Awareness, not just penalties: vendors often do not know the dyes are harmful; UP's guidelines suggest natural options (tomato, beetroot, Kashmiri chilli).
Food safety needs vendor awareness and safe substitutes, not only fines.
Category-specific rules: a colour allowed in cake is not allowed in chutney; safety depends on food type, quantity and heat.
Under FSSAI rules, a food colour is permitted only for specific foods and within set limits.
Enforcement gap: a strong law (fines up to ₹3 lakh, jail up to six months) but weak checks on the informal street-food sector.
India's food safety law is strong on paper, but enforcement in the informal street-food sector is weak.

examples: No colour in chutneys; no industrial dyes in cotton candy, kebabs or fish; vendors told to use natural ingredients

practice.q: Food adulteration is a silent public-health crisis in India. Discuss the challenges in enforcing food safety laws and suggest measures.
parts: Introduction: industrial dyes in UP's street food (one line, with facts)
Why adulteration is a public-health crisis

answer.t: In October 2026, UP found industrial dyes in chutneys and banned colours like Rhodamine-B in street food, despite the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

answer.h: Why it is a public-health crisis

pts.t: Banned dyes can cause liver damage and cancer over time.
Large doses poison; some dyes trigger allergic reactions.
Brightly coloured sweets and cotton candy target them.
Street food feeds millions daily, especially the poor.
Effects are slow, so the risk is underrated.
Beyond colours: spices, oils, milk and sweets are often adulterated.
pts.ex: Sudan dyes in oils and sauces.

pts.t: Millions of small vendors are hard to inspect.

pts.k: Too few food safety officers and labs
pts.t: Testing capacity is thin outside big cities.
Vendors often do not know a dye is harmful.
pts.ex: As a UP food safety officer noted.

pts.t: Industrial dyes are cheaper and brighter than food-grade colours.
Harsh action can hurt poor vendors.
Low conviction rates blunt the law.
Train vendors and promote natural colours.
pts.ex: UP's advice: beetroot, tomato, Kashmiri chilli.

pts.t: Expand food testing vans to small towns.
Scale clean street-food hubs with vendor training.
Track sale of industrial dyes at source.
Warn first-time small vendors; punish repeat and large offenders.
Simple home tests and complaint apps for citizens.

answer.t: Safe food needs aware vendors, strong labs and smart enforcement, so that public health is protected without crushing livelihoods.
